summary: VITA — Beyond Earth: Symptom Edition is a browser game that puts players in charge of four fictional crewmates on a 12-stage journey from Earth to Mars and back. Players compare a simulated cardiac-health index, review reports of hallucinations and bruising, and track accumulated radiation exposure. They inspect equipment, document observations, request crew support and respond to alerts while completing simplified launch, landing and docking tasks. A mission log and exportable report preserve what the crew observed and the actions it took. The project addresses the astronaut health monitoring challenge by giving players practice noticing changes, distinguishing reported symptoms from other indicators, and deciding when to involve the crew during a busy mission. NASA and Canadian Space Agency resources informed the scenarios. All values and flight controls are fictional and designed for education.
details:
What we built

VITA — Beyond Earth: Symptom Edition is an English-language browser simulation for the challenge Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions. Playing as mission commander, you monitor four fictional crewmates while completing 12 stages from Earth to Mars and back, including a fictional ISS handover. At each stage, an objectives list, equipment hotspots, crew status cards and a mission log help you decide what to do before advancing.

How monitoring works

The dashboard separates a fictional cardiac-health index, reported hallucinations, reported bruising and accumulated radiation exposure. Symptom scores come from scripted crew observations. Play involves comparing status, recording a report, requesting support and reviewing the assessment. A radiation alert asks you to select shelter and reassess. Recording a report or requesting support keeps the existing symptom scores visible. The game saves progress in the browser and exports a JSON mission report with the crew history and actions.

Design and impact

We wanted to make it easy to see what changes, where the information came from and which action comes next while handling competing priorities. The challenge brief, NASA Human Research Program and Canadian Space Agency references informed the risk scenarios. NASA crew-health, medical operations, exercise, ultrasound and dental references informed the broader research documented by the team. Real measurements and clinical protocols remain outside the scope of this educational prototype. The flight tasks are simplified exercises, the health values are fictional and radiation is expressed in relative game units.

Implementation and creative choices

The standalone game uses HTML, CSS, JavaScript, SVG illustrations and embedded artwork. It runs without a sign-in. We borrowed the idea of switching between exploration and management from Cult of the Lamb and drew inspiration for launch, landing and docking tasks from Kerbal Space Program. The earlier health-monitor and first-person prototypes helped us refine which observations, alerts and actions needed to be visible at each stage.

SI disclosure

The team reports using ChatGPT, Perplexity and Claude for ideation, research, writing, artwork and code assistance. The game labels SI-generated imagery and documents SI use and fictional data in its credits and metadata. The team also experimented with SI-generated music. The game links to the track externally and includes a player for optional, locally selected audio.
